grammarTopics.title: Present perfect simple
grammarTopics.explanation: Das present perfect verbindet Vergangenheit und Gegenwart. Du benutzt es, wenn es darum geht, OB etwas (schon einmal) passiert ist (Have you ever …?), ob etwas schon/gerade/noch nicht erledigt ist (already, just, not … yet) oder wenn das Ergebnis jetzt noch zu sehen ist. Bildung: have/has + past participle (regelmäßig -ed, unregelmäßig: 3. Spalte der Verbliste). Immer mit have/has – nie mit „sein" wie im Deutschen. never, ever, already, just stehen direkt nach have/has; yet steht am Satzende.
examples: Have you ever seen the London Marathon? – Of course I have.
Olivia has already prepared for the trials.
Gwen has just had an idea.
The girls haven't left for school yet.
I've hurt my foot. It hurts when I walk.
commonMistakes: „sein" aus dem Deutschen: „I'm left" statt „I've left"
simple past statt past participle: „I have went" statt „I have gone"
Wortstellung wie im Deutschen: „I have my foot hurt"

grammarTopics.title: Present perfect simple vs. simple past
grammarTopics.explanation: Present perfect: Es geht darum, DASS etwas passiert ist (ohne genaue Zeit, Ergebnis zählt; ever, never, already, just, yet). Simple past: Du berichtest genau, WANN etwas passiert ist. Mit genauen Zeitangaben wie yesterday, last week, three weeks ago, in 2019, when I was young steht nie das present perfect, sondern immer das simple past. Im Süddeutschen benutzt man fast nur das Perfekt – deshalb aufpassen!
examples: Have you seen Aunt Amy's new horse yet? – Yes, I have. She bought it last week.
I've already run in a marathon.
My dad ran in a marathon when he was 20.
I've been to London. I was there last year.
commonMistakes: present perfect mit genauer Zeitangabe: „I have seen it yesterday."
simple past bei ever/never/yet: „Did you ever play rugby?" (britisch: „Have you ever played …?")
Die Zeiten beliebig austauschen wie im Deutschen

grammarTopics.title: Timetable future (simple present mit Zukunftsbedeutung)
grammarTopics.explanation: Für feste Fahrpläne, Stundenpläne und Programme benutzt man auch für die Zukunft das simple present: The next bus leaves in twelve minutes. Das gilt nur für konkrete, festgelegte Zeiten (Abfahrt, Ankunft, Beginn eines Konzerts, Unterricht). he/she/it bekommt wie immer -s.
examples: The next bus leaves in twelve minutes.
Our train leaves at 9.15 a.m. from Platform 5.
The plane from New York arrives at 7 o'clock in the morning.
The concert starts tomorrow at 8 p.m.
commonMistakes: Timetable future für persönliche Pläne: „I visit my granny tomorrow." (besser: I'm going to visit …)

choices.feedback: Schönes Feedback! Frag gern noch nach: When did you win it?

choices.text: When have you won the Mini Marathon?
choices.feedback: Mit when (genauer Zeitpunkt) nimmst du das simple past: When did you win …?

n3.npcLine: I won it two years ago, when I was eleven. I was so proud!

choices.text: Have you already started training for this year's race?
choices.feedback: Super – already → present perfect.

choices.text: Do you train every day?
choices.feedback: Gute Frage! Auch möglich: Have you already started training?

choices.text: Did you already start training yet?
choices.feedback: Mit already/yet → present perfect: Have you already started training?

n4.npcLine: Yes, I have. I've already run 100 miles this month! But I haven't bought new running shoes yet.

choices.text: Thank you very much for the interview, Ayla. Good luck!
choices.feedback: Ein höflicher, runder Abschluss.

choices.text: OK, bye.
choices.feedback: Etwas höflicher zum Abschluss: Thank you for the interview!

choices.text: I have seen you in a race last year.
choices.feedback: last year → simple past: I saw you in a race last year.

n5.npcLine: You're welcome! See you at the race!

conversationScenarios.title: Radio-Reporter
conversationScenarios.goal: Sprache von Nachrichtenberichten, present perfect, past progressive
conversationScenarios.situation: Aliens sind im Greenwich Park gelandet! Du bist Reporterin beim Radio und interviewst einen aufgeregten Augenzeugen.
conversationScenarios.openingLine: Oh, hello! Are you from the radio? I've just seen something really strange in the park!
phrases: I've never seen anything like it!

n1.npcLine: Oh, hello! Are you from the radio? I've just seen something really strange in the park!

choices.text: Yes, I'm from Radio Greenwich. What have you seen?
choices.feedback: Profi-Reporterin – mit present perfect!

choices.text: Yes. What?
choices.feedback: Kurz, aber okay! Als Reporterin besser: What have you seen?

choices.text: What you have seen?
choices.feedback: In der Frage steht have vor dem Subjekt: What have you seen?

n2.npcLine: A spaceship! It has landed right next to the lake!

choices.text: What were you doing when the spaceship landed?
choices.feedback: Super – past progressive + simple past.

choices.text: Really? A spaceship?
choices.feedback: Gute Reaktion! Frag weiter: What were you doing when it landed?

choices.text: What did you doing when it landed?
choices.feedback: past progressive: What were you doing …?

n3.npcLine: I was walking my dog when there was a big flash. I couldn't believe my eyes!

choices.text: Have the aliens come out of the spaceship yet?
choices.feedback: Klasse Frage mit present perfect und yet!

choices.text: Did you see aliens?
choices.feedback: Gute Frage! Als Reporterin auch: Have the aliens come out yet?

choices.text: Have the aliens came out yet?
choices.feedback: come – came – come → Have the aliens come out yet?

n4.npcLine: Yes! Three little green aliens have just walked to the ice cream van. I've never seen anything like it!

choices.text: Thank you. This is Juna for Radio Greenwich. Back to the studio!
choices.feedback: Ein echter Radio-Abschluss!

choices.text: Wow. Thanks.
choices.feedback: Ein Radiobericht braucht einen Abschluss: This is … for Radio Greenwich.

choices.text: I am never see anything like it!
choices.feedback: present perfect: I've never seen anything like it!

n5.npcLine: Oh look – they're buying ice cream! Aliens love ice cream!

conversationScenarios.title: Nach dem Weg fragen in London
conversationScenarios.situation: Du stehst an der Victoria Station und fragst eine Passantin nach dem Weg zu Buckingham Palace und zum London Eye.
conversationScenarios.openingLine: You look a bit lost. Can I help you?
phrases: Excuse me, how do I get to …?
When does the next train leave?

n1.npcLine: You look a bit lost. Can I help you?

choices.text: Yes, please. Excuse me, how do I get to Buckingham Palace?
choices.feedback: Höflich und genau richtig gefragt!

choices.text: Buckingham Palace?
choices.feedback: Verständlich! Höflicher: Excuse me, how do I get to Buckingham Palace?

choices.text: Where is Buckingham Palace? Tell me.
choices.feedback: Das klingt zu direkt. Besser: Excuse me, how do I get to …?

n2.npcLine: Sure. Go out of the station and turn right. Then go straight on. The palace is at the end of the road. It's about ten minutes on foot.

choices.text: So I turn right and then go straight on. Thank you!
choices.feedback: Super – du wiederholst den Weg zur Kontrolle.

choices.text: Ten minutes? OK.
choices.feedback: Gut! Zur Sicherheit kannst du den Weg wiederholen: So I turn right …

choices.text: So I turn left and go straight on.
choices.feedback: Hör noch mal genau hin: turn right.

n3.npcLine: You're welcome. Are you going to see the London Eye too?

choices.text: Yes, I am. When does the next train to Waterloo leave?
choices.feedback: Perfekt – Kurzantwort und Frage im timetable future.

choices.text: Yes.
choices.feedback: Mit Kurzantwort: Yes, I am.

choices.text: Yes, I do.
choices.feedback: Die Frage beginnt mit Are → Yes, I am.

n4.npcLine: The next train leaves at 2.15 from Platform 3. You can buy a ticket at the ticket machine over there.

choices.text: Thank you! Is a return ticket cheaper than two single tickets?
choices.feedback: Kluge Frage mit Vergleich (cheaper than)!

choices.text: OK. Bye.
choices.feedback: Ein Dankeschön ist höflicher: Thank you very much!

choices.text: The next train leave at 2.15?
choices.feedback: train = it → leaves: The next train leaves at 2.15.

n5.npcLine: Yes, a return ticket is usually cheaper. Enjoy London!
